title: GGUF LLM Models with Hidden Malware on Hugging Face Reached 2400 Victims
author: homarp
snippet: 1. Summary Local LLMs are usually shared as GGUF files, and every GGUF file carries a chat template that the runtime applies to each prompt. Chat template poisoning abuses that template. The model answers normally, while the template quietly adds instructions the user never…
excerpt: 1. Summary Local LLMs are usually shared as GGUF files, and every GGUF file carries a chat template that the runtime applies to each prompt. Chat template poisoning abuses that template. The model answers normally, while the template quietly adds instructions the user never sees: make an agent run a PowerShell command, or open every reply with a command for the user to run. In its strongest form, the malicious program travels inside the model file itself, appended after the last tensor where loaders never read, and the template is switched on later. A scan of all 3273389 public Hugging Face model repositories on 26 November 2026 found 5 malicious GGUF models with 2428 downloads as of 27 November. Hugging Face counts downloads, not people, so the number of affected users is lower or equal. The largest campaign, Mir2k, uploaded two uncensored GGUF models with a Windows remote access trojan named ollie hidden at the end of each file, and on 26 November rewrote both templates so the model asks the user to run the line that unpacks it. The open-source tool gguf-radar detects these templates and hidden bytes without running anything, and rebuilds a clean GGUF file with the model weights unchanged. Indicators, YARA rules and a MITRE mapping close the post. The key figures of the scan are summarized below; each one is explained in Section 3. The scan in numbers - public model repositories scanned - 3.27 million - malicious models still online - 5 repos - downloads of those models - 2428 - actors behind them - 2 If one of these models was downloaded Check endpoints against the indicators in Section 7.2 and scan local .gguf files with gguf-radar. Antivirus engines and checks that only look at the last few kilobytes of a file do not see the compressed payload. 2. Attack Mechanics A GGUF file has a simple layout. A header and a metadata table come first, the tensor table follows, then padding up to an alignment boundary, and finally the model weights. Runtimes such as…

excerpt: ggml : add CONCAT backward pass (#32151) Each input's gradient is a view of the output gradient at its offset along dim, made contiguous. Mark a and b as params so grad mode checks the op, with grad_nmax raised to 40000 to keep the default shapes. The output is weighted by random values in [1, 2], since with a plain sum every gradient is 1 and a wrong offset would still pass. Transposed-b cases are not grad checked, they only cover the forward. excerpt: chat : Allow K2 Horizon tool call during thought (#32993) Allow tool calls that would otherwise appear inside reasoning/thinking blocks for K2 Horizon. K2 Horizon models can emit tool calls without closing the thinking block. Without this fix the parser would only stop on explicit end tag, and the tool call was lost without executing. With this PR we now end reasoning before the tool call starts. In short, when reasoning mentions <ifm|tool_calls>, we end reasoning there. My tests cover this case at medium and high effort. This fixes #32972, and is the same pattern as #32232 (Gemma4) and #32271 (Ministral-3). I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines I have used Opus to run and score benchmarks, help find the K2 parser, draft the fix and test, and see how others have resolved this for other models. I have carefully examined all changes and tested with my local benchmarks. I have used Sol to code review twice. title: Ask HN: Is anyone using Gemini Live (3.8) in scaled production
author: aenis
snippet: I am considering moving our voice stack from a cascaded model to voice-to-voice. I have been burned by the first versions of Gemini Live a year ago, and I was wondering how is it to run the current model, 3.8, in real production these days. Our voice workloads average at around…
excerpt: I am considering moving our voice stack from a cascaded model to voice-to-voice. I have been burned by the first versions of Gemini Live a year ago, and I was wondering how is it to run the current model, 3.8, in real production these days. Our voice workloads average at around 100 conversations in parallel, spiking to less than 1k every now and then. The main reason for moving to voice-to-voice is refactoring of an old codebase; the current engine requires a do-over anyway, so I am debating whether staying at STT/LLM/TTS cascade still is the best choice. I built a fully functioning port, it performs well in demos, but so did the earlier versions. And since my voice ai guru, Kwindla Kramer of Daily, is still not writing about voice to voice often, I have a suspicion those models are not yet at 'sleep well at night while running this at scale' level. Any feedback, observations and real world experiences would be most welcome.

Status: v0.2.2, validated on open models (see docs/WRITEUP.md). v0.2.1 added correct chunking of Claude Code–style traces and audits reported causes on fresh replays (family-wise error ≤ α). v0.2.2 tells a rule that makes the agent act and picks what it does from one that only makes it act, by replaying with the tool forced. uvx ctxblame --help # or: pip install ctxblame Real v0.2.1 trace (real/run1/step21, Qwen3-14B on local vLLM): ctxblame separates the edit_file precondition, catches all 3 redundant --tb=line carriers that leave-one-out misses (5/5 kept alone), and certifies the bundle on 20 fresh replays (p = 1.9e-6, 91% KV-cache hit). The examples below use uv run ctxblame from a checkout; uvx ctxblame works the same. Two wire formats are supported, which covers most models: Anthropic Messages (/v1/messages) and OpenAI Chat Completions (/chat/completions). The simplest way is to wrap the agent command: uv run ctxblame wrap -- claude -p "fix the failing test" # or any agent command wrap starts two recording proxies on free local ports (Anthropic and OpenAI format) and runs the command with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and OPENAI_BASE_URL pointing at them. Base URLs you have already set become the upstreams, so an agent pointed at DeepSeek or a local vLLM server keeps using it (or pass --anthropic-upstream / --openai-upstream). Only clients that read these variables are captured; calls to other APIs (e.g. the OpenAI Responses API) are forwarded but not recorded. author: MaxTeabag
snippet: I’ve been trying to make more of my daily life AI-driven, and my iPhone was becoming the bottleneck. If an app didn’t have a web version, an MCP, or an API, I still had to pick up the phone and do it myself. After lots of searching I finally found a solution that worked. I put…
excerpt: I’ve been trying to make more of my daily life AI-driven, and my iPhone was becoming the bottleneck. If an app didn’t have a web version, an MCP, or an API, I still had to pick up the phone and do it myself. After lots of searching I finally found a solution that worked. I put a spare iPhone in developer mode, installed WebDriverAgent, and left it on my home Wi-Fi. WebDriverAgent is built on Apple’s official UI testing framework. It’s literally computer use for iPhone. I tried mirroring the screen with AirPlay and even streaming a camera, but nothing beat WebDriverAgent. Stock WebDriverAgent was still slow in a lot of apps, so I patched it and had an agent keep improving it by trying it across tons of apps. That became Turbotap. Now I can just ask AI to change a setting, stress-test my app on a real iPhone, or do something in an app I used to have to do by hand. Honestly, I built it out of irritation and increasing inflammation in my hands, but it’s unlocked so many things I can automate with LLMs. The AI can use the actual iPhone app the same way I would, even if there’s no web version, MCP, or API. That’s why I’m excited to share it. You need Xcode on a Mac to sign and install WebDriverAgent over USB. Once it’s running, you can drive the phone headlessly from a Mac or Linux machine on the same Wi-Fi. It’s free and open source.

excerpt: November 2026 edition How AI like ChatGPT works, updated every month Most of us use AI tools every day without knowing what happens between typing a question and getting an answer. This guide explains it from the ground up, in plain language, with diagrams you can try. Here for security? Start with prompt injection (14 min, no earlier chapters needed). Your text, as tokens Through the layers Next-token probabilities Part 1: Language models How a language model turns text into numbers, predicts the next word and learns from data, and where that breaks down. Each chapter has a demo to try and three questions at the end. New to this? Start with chapter 1; otherwise jump around. What an LLM is, in five minutes The whole picture in five minutes: what these systems are, how they were built and what they are not. Text becomes tokens, tokens become numbers Models never see letters or words. They see numbered pieces of text, and then points on a map of meaning. Attention: how words borrow meaning How each word looks back at the earlier words and pulls in what it needs. This is the core mechanism of the transformer. Inside the stack Each layer gathers context from other words and then processes it, and a model repeats that dozens of times. Also: the trick that lets giant models run cheaply. Generating text, one token at a time Each word is a weighted dice roll. That explains why answers differ every time, what "temperature" does and why thinking takes time. Assembled directly with nasm and linked with ld. Every math kernel (expf, sincosf, RMSNorm, RoPE, SiLU, Softmax), AVX2+FMA+F16C GEMM/GEMV engine, BPE tokenizer, clone()/futex() thread pool, bare-metal SMP kernel, analytical backward pass, AdamW optimizer, and live Unicode Braille TUI is hand-written x86-64 assembly (17,252 lines total across all three projects). title: Estimating LLM decode speed and the price of a token per second
author: lrsaturnino
snippet: Build Finder: estimating LLM decode speed and the price of a token per second A per-operation model calibrated on public benchmarks, corrected for concurrent sessions with measured runs, and checked on machines it never saw Abstract Build Finder lists every hardware build that…
excerpt: Build Finder: estimating LLM decode speed and the price of a token per second A per-operation model calibrated on public benchmarks, corrected for concurrent sessions with measured runs, and checked on machines it never saw Abstract Build Finder lists every hardware build that runs a chosen open-weight language model at a target decode speed, cheapest per token per second (tok/s) first: the price of the whole build divided by its speed. Its catalog holds 273 GPUs, used as 1 to 8 cards, 619 CPUs and 333 complete systems, at dated US prices. Speeds come from a per-operation model: each operation of a token's pass takes the longer of reading its bytes and doing its arithmetic, at efficiencies and engine costs fitted per engine and hardware family to 424 one-session benchmarks from 120 devices. For several sessions at once, a correction with two parameters per engine, model kind and session range is fitted to 418 measured runs on 19 machines. Against the 427 measured decode runs the page lists without speculative decoding, the median estimate is 11% below the measured speed on NVIDIA hardware (385 runs), 1.43 times the measured speed on Macs (31 runs) and 1.73 times the measured speed on Inkling 2 Mini (11 runs). On the GeForce RTX 3090, which neither fit has seen on llama.cpp (CUDA), 87% of 54 runs fall within 1.25 times the measured speed and 100% within 1.5 times. Runs with speculative decoding, which the estimates leave out, measured a median 2.3 times the estimate. We describe the data, the model, the fit, its validation and what the estimates cannot yet capture. 1Introduction Running an open-weight model on one's own hardware starts with a buying question: which machine gives the decode speed a use needs, and what does it cost? The evidence people find is scattered across benchmark threads, engine READMEs and forum posts, each for one card, one engine, one model file and usually one session, often without the details needed to compare them, while prices move…
